seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #9 — uv.lock Explained (and Why uv sync Deletes Things) (2026)
altTitles: The uv lockfile: hashes, universal resolution and --exact
seo.description: Chapter nine of the uv course. Locking versus syncing, what is really inside uv.lock, why a sha256 beats a version number, universal cross-platform resolution, --locked and --frozen for CI, and why uv sync removes packages you installed behind its back.
seo.breakdown: why the lockfile records exact bytes rather than version numbers, and why uv sync removes anything it did not record.

scenes.narration: It works on your machine. It fails on theirs. Same code, same command.

Your pyproject says rich greater-than-or-equal-to fifteen. You installed it in March, and got fifteen point zero. Your colleague clones the repo in June, when sixteen is out, and gets sixteen. Same file, two different sets of packages. So what stops the drift?

uvStage.headline: Same file, [different] packages
uvStage.premise: A range is a permission, not an instruction. Two people can both obey it differently.

steps.label: grep rich pyproject.toml
steps.detail: a floor. anything above it is allowed.

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter is about the file that makes two machines identical, and about the one uv behaviour that genuinely startles people coming from pip.

data.title: The lockfile
data.subtitle: uv, chapter nine · exact bytes, not version numbers

scenes.narration: Start by separating two words that get used interchangeably and mean different things.

Locking is deciding. Given your requirements, uv works out one exact set of versions that satisfies all of them, then writes the decision down. Syncing is doing: uv reads that decision and makes your folder match it. Two separate jobs, and keeping the two apart is what makes the whole arrangement reliable.

uvStage.headline: Deciding, then [doing]
uvStage.premise: Lock writes down one exact answer. Sync makes your folder match that answer.

steps.label: uv lock
steps.detail: decided, and written down

steps.label: uv sync
steps.detail: done — and Checked means already correct

scenes.narration: You'll almost never type uv lock yourself, though, because every command that touches your environment locks first. Adding a package locks. Running your code locks. Syncing locks. So the file stays correct without anybody maintaining anything, which is rather the point of the design.

uvStage.headline: You rarely [type] it yourself
uvStage.premise: Every command that touches the environment locks first, so the file stays current.

steps.label: uv run main.py
steps.detail: it locked, checked and ran, in one line

stage.label: uv lock
stage.sub: and all three do this one first

scenes.narration: Open the file, because there's a field in it doing more work than you'd expect.

Here's a real entry. A name, a version, where the package came from, and then a hash — sha256, followed by sixty-four characters. The hash isn't decoration. A version number tells you which release arrived; a hash tells you which exact bytes arrived. Those are genuinely different promises.

uvStage.headline: A version, and a [seal]
uvStage.premise: A version names a release. A hash names the exact file, byte for byte.

steps.label: head -12 uv.lock
steps.detail: the hash is the interesting field

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: the same bytes on every machine, or none

scenes.narration: Why does the difference matter? Because a version number can in principle be re-uploaded, and because any download can be corrupted or intercepted on the way. A hash catches both problems. If the bytes arriving don't match the recorded hash, uv refuses to install rather than hoping for the best.

uvStage.headline: The hash is a [check], not a label
uvStage.premise: If the bytes arriving do not match the recorded hash, uv stops rather than hoping.

steps.label: uv sync
out: Caused by: Hash mismatch for rich==15.0.0
steps.detail: refused. not installed-and-hoped-for.

scenes.narration: The lockfile is also universal, which is a genuinely unusual property. One file covers every platform — Windows, macOS, Linux, several Python versions — so a colleague on a different operating system resolves from your file rather than needing one of their own.

uvStage.headline: One file, [every] platform
uvStage.premise: The same lockfile answers for Windows, macOS and Linux, and several Pythons.

steps.label: grep -c "resolution-markers" uv.lock
steps.detail: four platform answers, in one file

stage.label: colorama
stage.sub: and the markers say who gets it

scenes.narration: And now the behaviour that surprises everybody who arrives from pip.

I installed typer behind uv's back, using the pip interface. Then I ran a plain uv sync. Watch what happened: uv uninstalled three packages nobody asked it to touch. Not a bug — sync is exact by default, and exact means the folder must match the lockfile, with nothing extra sitting alongside.

uvStage.headline: uv sync [removes] extras
uvStage.premise: Exact means the folder matches the lockfile. Anything else is an extra, and goes.

steps.label: uv pip install typer
steps.detail: installed behind uv’s back, on purpose

steps.label: uv sync
steps.detail: three gone, and nobody asked for that

stage.label: the lockfile
stage.sub: and the folder now matches exactly

scenes.narration: Which sounds alarming, and is precisely the point. If uv left extras alone, your environment would slowly fill with packages nobody ever recorded, and sooner or later one such package would be the reason something broke. Exact means the folder always tells the truth about the file.

uvStage.headline: Alarming, and [correct]
uvStage.premise: An environment that keeps extras drifts. An exact one always matches the file.

steps.label: uv sync --inexact
steps.detail: if you really want extras left alone

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: and nothing can drift in between them

scenes.narration: Three flags matter on a build machine. Locked fails if the lockfile is out of date, which is exactly what you want in continuous integration — a refusal beats a helpful silent update. Frozen uses the file as it stands and never re-resolves. And no-sync locks without touching your environment at all.

uvStage.headline: Three flags for [CI]
uvStage.premise: On a build machine you want a refusal, not a helpful silent update.

steps.label: uv sync --locked
out: error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated,
steps.detail: the build fails, which is correct here

steps.label: uv run --frozen main.py
steps.detail: use the file as-is, never re-resolve

steps.label: uv lock --no-sync
steps.detail: decide, without touching the folder

scenes.narration: One more thing's worth knowing, because it surprises people in the opposite direction. New releases are ignored until you explicitly ask for them. A newer rich comes out, and nothing happens — no automatic upgrade, no quiet drift. You ask, or the version stays exactly where it is.

uvStage.headline: New releases are [ignored]
uvStage.premise: A newer version existing is not a reason to change anything. You have to ask.

steps.label: uv sync
steps.detail: rich 16 is out. nothing happened.

steps.label: uv lock --upgrade-package rich
steps.detail: and now, because you asked

scenes.narration: A fair question at this point: when does the lockfile actually go stale? The answer's narrower than most people expect. Changing a requirement so the locked version no longer qualifies makes it stale. Loosening a constraint that still allows the locked version does not, because the recorded answer is still a valid one.

uvStage.headline: When it goes [stale]
uvStage.premise: Stale means the recorded answer is no longer allowed — not merely no longer newest.

steps.label: uv add "rich>=14" && uv lock --check
steps.detail: looser, and 15.0.0 still qualifies

steps.label: uv add "rich>=16" && uv lock --check
out: error: The lockfile needs to be updated
steps.detail: now the locked answer is not allowed

scenes.narration: It's also worth saying plainly what the lockfile is not. Nobody edits the file by hand. uv.lock is generated, regenerated constantly, and any hand edit gets overwritten by the next command you run. Treat the file as output — read it, review it in a pull request, and never type into it.

uvStage.headline: Read it. Never [edit] it.
uvStage.premise: Generated output, regenerated constantly. A hand edit lasts until the next command.

steps.label: sed -i "s/15.0.0/99.0.0/" uv.lock && uv sync
steps.detail: your edit lasted exactly one command

stage.label: reviewing it
stage.sub: yes — a diff shows every version change

stage.label: editing it
stage.sub: no — the next command overwrites you

scenes.narration: And the diff is genuinely useful in review. Because uv.lock is text, and every entry carries a version and a hash, a pull request bumping one dependency shows exactly which packages moved and which stayed put — considerably better than trusting a summary line in a commit message.

uvStage.headline: The diff is the [review]
uvStage.premise: Plain text, one entry per package, so a version bump is visible line by line.

steps.label: git diff --stat uv.lock
steps.detail: six lines changed, out of four hundred

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: one package moved, twelve did not

scenes.narration: Quick check. You pip-install something into a uv project, then run uv sync. What happens to that package? Pause the video here and decide before I say anything. Ready? uv removes it, because sync is exact and the package is not in the lockfile.

quiz.question: pip-installed a package, then ran uv sync. What happens?

options.text: uv removes it — sync is exact
uv adds it to the lockfile

quiz.why: Not in the lockfile means not in the folder. --inexact opts out.

scenes.narration: So commit the lockfile. That one file turns works-on-my-machine into works-everywhere, it's plain text so a code review can actually read it, and it costs you nothing at all, because uv keeps the file correct on your behalf.

uvStage.headline: Commit it, and [stop] worrying
uvStage.premise: The same thirteen packages, the same thirteen hashes, on both machines.

steps.label: git clone ... && uv sync
steps.detail: sixty-two milliseconds to identical

stage.label: pytest
stage.sub: the same exact bytes, on both machines

scenes.narration: So, to recap. Locking decides one exact set of versions and writes them down with their hashes. Syncing makes your folder match, exactly, removing anything that isn't recorded. And nothing upgrades until you explicitly ask for it.

points.text: Lock decides. Sync does. Different jobs.
A hash says which bytes, not which release
sync is exact — extras are removed

scenes.narration: Next chapter, what happens when two packages want versions that cannot both be true, and how uv explains its own refusal in plain English.
